analysis.one_liner: Repeals six tax breaks for oil and gas producers.
analysis.headline: The bill repealing oil and gas tax breaks was introduced in the Senate in May 2009, sent to the Finance Committee, and never received a hearing, vote, or cosponsor before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would strip away six long-standing tax advantages enjoyed by oil and gas companies: the domestic production deduction, the credit for pumping from marginal wells, the loophole that lets investors in oil and gas treat income as active, the fast write-off for exploration costs, the deduction for intangible drilling costs, and the percentage depletion allowance. Ending these breaks would raise federal revenue, which the bill does not direct to any specific use. Its committee took no action, so it never reached the Senate floor.
analysis.who_benefits: Federal taxpayers as a whole, because closing these tax breaks would bring in more revenue and reduce the deficit if not spent elsewhere. Competing energy sources, including renewables, would face less of a tax-code tilt toward oil and gas. The bill's sponsor framed it as ending special treatment for a mature, profitable industry.

how_it_helps.text: The bill repeals the deduction for income from domestic oil and gas production under section 199, a break available to almost no other manufacturer after 2005.

It terminates the credit for producing oil and gas from marginal wells, repeals the exception that lets oil and gas working-interest owners escape passive-loss limits, stretches the write-off period for exploration costs from two years to seven, ends the immediate deduction of intangible drilling costs, and sets the percentage depletion allowance for oil and gas wells to zero.
The provisions apply to taxable years beginning after enactment, so the changes take effect immediately rather than being phased out over many years.

analysis.who_pays: Oil and gas producers, from large integrated companies to independent drillers and operators of small marginal wells, would pay more federal tax. Part of the cost could reach consumers if producers pass higher after-tax costs into fuel prices, though most of these breaks lower taxes on income already earned rather than directly subsidizing the price at the pump.
analysis.who_pays_short: Oil and gas producers, possibly consumers

drawbacks.text: Repealing exploration and drilling tax deductions raises the after-tax cost of domestic drilling, which independent economists and the industry argue would reduce domestic production and could nudge fuel prices up for consumers.
The bill raises revenue but designates no use for it, so it is silent on whether the money reduces the deficit or funds something else.

Small operators of marginal wells, which produce low volumes from nearly exhausted wells, would lose a credit specifically designed for them, and some such wells could become uneconomic and be plugged.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: On balance the bill would close tax breaks that give oil and gas income tax treatment no other industry gets, at the cost of somewhat higher after-tax drilling expenses and a possible small effect on domestic output and consumer prices. It was a straightforward revenue measure rather than a subsidy for anything, and its main weakness is that it never says what the money is for.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate sent the bill to the Finance Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never scheduled it for anything, and it died when the Congress ended in January 2011.

narrative.text: Senator John Kerry introduced the bill on May 20, 2009, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance the same day.
No senator signed on as a cosponsor at any point.
The Finance Committee took no further action on the bill; there was no hearing, markup, or committee vote recorded, and the full Senate never considered it.
The bill expired when the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011, without a floor vote in either chamber.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil and gas producers kept all six tax breaks, worth billions of dollars a year across the industry, because the bill never advanced. The Treasury forgoes the revenue the repeal would have raised, and taxpayers who would benefit from that revenue are no better off.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Oil and gas producers kept their tax breaks

for.name: Sen. John Kerry
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on it.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee (Chair Max Baucus)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on the day it was introduced and never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote; the bill died in committee.

against.name: Oil and gas industry
against.what_they_did: Opposed repeal of the section 199 domestic production deduction and other oil and gas tax provisions, which were preserved through the 111th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: There was never a vote or recorded position beyond the Democratic sponsor and zero cosponsors, so no partisan split can be measured from the record.

industries.note: The bill would eliminate six tax preferences these companies currently enjoy, including the domestic production deduction and percentage depletion, raising their federal tax bills. Their interest in keeping the breaks runs against taxpayers, who bear the revenue cost.

Small operators pumping low-volume wells would lose the section 45I credit created specifically for marginal wells, and some marginal wells could become unprofitable. The credit's benefit is concentrated on this narrow group rather than on consumers.

The bill ends the immediate deduction of intangible drilling costs and stretches the write-off for geological and geophysical exploration spending from two years to seven, increasing the cost of financing exploration. This affects domestic drilling activity, which can feed back into fuel prices.
